edition.sessionCovered: Thu, Nov 12 (Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO — NVDA -4.3% · Gold $3,876 as 10Y breaks 5.10% · Brent $95.82 on Houthi Saudi attacks · BTC $72,000)
edition.fomc: Next: 8–9 Dec (25bp hike near certain; ~18% odds of 50bp)
edition.stripNote: Fri 13 Nov. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday — NVDA fell as much as 14% intraday before closing 4.3% lower at $166.19; CFO Colette Kress named interim CEO. Gold plunged 2.8% to $3,876 as the 10-year Treasury yield broke above 5% for the first time to 5.10%, its highest since late 2023. Brent crude surged 3.7% to $95.82 after Houthi forces struck Saudi pipeline infrastructure, an oil facility in Yanbu and an Aramco building in Riyadh; Iran's military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz. Silver fell 3.7% to $49.93. WTI settled at $88.74 (+2.9%). The dollar index reached a 19-month high. Equities declined: S&P 7,592 (−0.4%), Dow 52,297 (−0.4%), Nasdaq 25,366 (−0.4%). Bitcoin fell to approximately $72,000 — its weakest since August — extending the selloff to six consecutive weeks in the red. Grains sold off sharply: wheat −2.6% to 584¼¢, corn −1.5% to 442½¢, soybeans −0.9% to 1,219¢. Ukraine drones hit Russia's Ust-Luga Baltic coast port, causing fires at fuel storage tanks. The November 27 gallium/germanium/antimony deadline is 14 days away. APEC meets in Shenzhen Nov 18–19.

overview: Thursday's session was dominated by three converging shocks: the sudden resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the 10-year Treasury yield breaking above 5% for the first time, and a fresh escalation in the Middle East. Gold plunged 2.8% to approximately $3,876 per ounce — its third straight day of selling since Tuesday's hot CPI print — as the 10-year yield surged to 5.10% and the dollar index hit a 19-month high. Silver fell even harder, down 3.7% to $49.93, losing its industrial-demand cushion as the broader risk mood soured. Oil moved sharply in the opposite direction: Brent crude settled at $95.82 per barrel, up 3.7%, after Houthi forces attacked a Saudi East-West pipeline pumping station, an oil facility in Yanbu and an Aramco building in Riyadh. Iran's military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz. Ukraine's drones struck Russia's Ust-Luga Baltic port, damaging fuel storage tanks. US equities fell modestly — S&P 500 at 7,592 (−0.4%), Nasdaq at 25,366 (−0.4%) — absorbing both the Nvidia shock and the rate headwind. Nvidia itself dropped as much as 14% intraday before recovering to close 4.3% lower at $166.19; the company named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. CME FedWatch continues to price a 25-basis-point hike at the December 8–9 FOMC as near certain, with approximately 18% odds of 50 basis points.

Grains sold off sharply on Thursday as the surging dollar and rising Treasury yields overwhelmed the post-WASDE bullish tailwind. Wheat fell 2.6% to 584¼¢ per bushel, reversing Wednesday's break above 600¢. Corn dropped 1.5% to 442½¢ and soybeans eased 0.9% to 1,219¢. SovEcon cut its Russian wheat export estimate to 36 million tonnes, below the USDA's 39 million tonne forecast. Base metals were mixed: copper fell 1.4% to $6.17 per pound ($13,605 per tonne LME) on the stronger dollar, while zinc eased 0.8% to $3,726 per tonne. Nickel was nearly flat at $16,230 and tin rose 0.3% to $46,652 on tight LME inventories. Platinum fell 0.8% to $1,526 and palladium dropped 3.1% to $1,008, tracking gold's decline. Bitcoin fell to approximately $72,000 — its weakest level since August — as the hawkish rates environment continued to weigh; Ethereum dropped to $1,993. Cocoa rebounded above $5,200 per tonne as Ivory Coast's national weather agency (Sodexam) projected 2026/27 output could drop 21–25% due to an 'exceptionally strong El Niño event.' Coal firmed to $142 per tonne Newcastle, supported by LNG supply tightness. The November 27 export-control deadline for gallium, germanium and antimony is now 14 days away; APEC meets in Shenzhen November 18–19.

watchItems.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO — biggest corporate shock in years
watchItems.text: Nvidia announced Thursday that Jensen Huang resigned as president, CEO and director, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor. Longtime director Harvey C. Jones became the board's first-ever chair. The resignation followed weeks of scrutiny over Huang's personal relationships and reported board discussions about removing him. NVDA fell as much as 14% intraday — briefly wiping over $400 billion in market cap — before recovering to close 4.3% lower at $166.19. Citigroup cut its Nvidia price target from $285 to $225. The stock has now lost approximately $1.7 trillion in value since October. The leadership vacuum at the world's most valuable semiconductor company raises immediate questions about AI infrastructure buildout timelines, customer relationships and the pace of GPU product launches. The broader Nasdaq fell just 0.4%, suggesting the market is treating this as company-specific rather than sector-wide.

watchItems.title: 10-year Treasury yield breaks 5% for the first time — gold hammered below $3,900
watchItems.text: The 10-year Treasury yield broke above 5% on Thursday, settling at approximately 5.10% — a level not seen since late 2023. The 2-year yield rose to 4.86%. The move extended the post-CPI selloff that began on Tuesday and hammered gold below $3,900 for the first time, with bullion settling near $3,876 per ounce, down 2.8%. Silver fell even harder at 3.7% to $49.93. The dollar index surged to a 19-month high, pressuring dollar-denominated commodities across the board. CME FedWatch now prices approximately 18% odds of a 50-basis-point hike at the December 8–9 FOMC. The 30-year bond auction earlier this week came at a yield of 5.618%. The yield breakout above 5% is a critical threshold for risk assets — it raises the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets like gold and crypto, strengthens the dollar, and pressures emerging-market borrowers.

watchItems.title: Brent surges 3.7% to $95.82 on Houthi Saudi attacks and Hormuz tanker explosions
watchItems.text: Brent crude settled at $95.82 per barrel on Thursday, up 3.7%, after a series of attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure. Yemen's Houthi forces claimed strikes on a pumping station on the Saudi East-West pipeline, an oil facility in Yanbu and an Aramco building in Riyadh. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two Houthi drones. Separately, Iran's military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz after 'ignoring warnings.' WTI settled at $88.74, up 2.9%. Ukraine's drones also hit Russia's Ust-Luga Baltic coast port, causing fires at fuel storage tanks. Trump said Washington 'did not need a deal' with Iran, declaring 'we've got their strait.' OPEC+ data showed October crude output rose, led by Saudi Arabia. Despite the geopolitical escalation, both Brent and WTI remain about 2.5% lower for the week.

watchItems.title: China export-control deadline 14 days away — APEC provides a diplomatic window
watchItems.text: The November 27 deadline — when the suspension of China's export prohibition on gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials to the US expires — is now 14 days away. The November 10 lapse of the broader Announcement No. 70 package, covering rare earth equipment, technology and five additional rare earths, has already passed with no published extension. APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen November 18–19, providing a narrow diplomatic window for a possible Trump–Xi discussion on the deadline. Gallium remains at approximately $2,100 per kilogram outside China versus $460 domestically — a 4.5x premium. Antimony holds at ¥93,500 per tonne in China. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken FID but is not yet producing. On the cobalt front, Glencore reportedly won a US government contract to supply up to $900 million of cobalt over five years for strategic stockpiles.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: Third straight selloff since CPI · broke below $3,900 · 10Y yield broke 5.10% · dollar at 19-month high · COMEX low $3,857
desk.sum: Gold plunged 2.8% to approximately $3,876 per ounce on Thursday — its third consecutive session of selling since Tuesday's hot CPI print. The 10-year Treasury yield broke above 5% for the first time to approximately 5.10%, dramatically raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion. The dollar index surged to a 19-month high. COMEX gold hit an intraday low of $3,857. Gold has now fallen over 6% in three sessions. CME FedWatch prices approximately 18% odds of a 50-basis-point hike at the December FOMC. The 30-year bond auction came at 5.618%. Central bank buying remains supportive at 675 tonnes year to date, but the combined force of surging yields, a stronger dollar and fading geopolitical safe-haven demand from US–Iran diplomacy is overwhelming.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: Fell harder than gold · lost industrial cushion · broke below $50 for first time since mid-October
desk.sum: Silver fell 3.7% to $49.93 per ounce on Thursday, underperforming even gold's decline and breaking below the $50 level for the first time since mid-October. The metal's dual precious-industrial profile failed to provide its usual relative support as the broader commodity complex came under pressure from the surging dollar and Treasury yields above 5%. The gold-silver ratio widened as silver fell faster. The three-day selloff since Tuesday's CPI has erased more than $4 from silver's price. Solar panel demand remains structurally supportive, but with the dollar at a 19-month high and rates surging, the macro headwind is overpowering fundamental support.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $88.74 · Houthi attacks on Saudi pipeline, Yanbu, Aramco Riyadh · 4 tankers hit by explosions in Hormuz · Ukraine drones hit Ust-Luga
desk.sum: Brent crude surged 3.7% to $95.82 per barrel on Thursday after a series of attacks escalated the Middle East conflict. Houthi forces struck a pumping station on the Saudi East-West pipeline, an oil facility in Yanbu and an Aramco building in Riyadh. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two drones. Iran's military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz after 'ignoring warnings.' WTI settled at $88.74, up 2.9%. Ukraine's drones hit Russia's Ust-Luga Baltic coast port, damaging fuel storage. Trump said Washington did not need a deal with Iran, declaring 'we've got their strait.' OPEC+ data showed October crude output rising. Despite the surge, both benchmarks remain about 2.5% lower for the week.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME $13,605/t · dollar at 19-month high pressures · Yangshan premium still elevated · SHFE stocks depleted
desk.sum: Copper fell 1.4% to $6.17 per pound ($13,605 per tonne LME 3M) on Thursday as the surging dollar and Treasury yields above 5% pressured base metals. The dollar index hit a 19-month high, raising the cost of dollar-denominated commodities for non-US buyers. The Yangshan copper import premium remains elevated, signalling continued Chinese physical demand, and SHFE stocks remain depleted at approximately 60,000 mt. But the macro headwind from the hawkish rates environment overpowered the constructive supply picture. LME session volume was 23,000 lots with open interest falling by 4,425 lots, suggesting some long liquidation.

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Firmed to $142 · LNG still elevated at ~$32 JKM · QatarEnergy FM through year-end · energy demand substitution continues
desk.sum: Newcastle coal firmed to $142 per tonne, up approximately 2.2%, as the broader energy complex tightened. Oil's 3.7% surge on Saudi and Hormuz attacks supported the energy sector, while continued LNG supply tightness keeps coal demand elevated as a baseload alternative. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, and the IEA projects 2026 global LNG output will fall about 3%. EU storage sits below the five-year average ahead of winter. The stronger dollar is a mild headwind for seaborne coal pricing, but the supply-side fundamentals remain supportive.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Eased modestly tracking gold · industrial demand limiting downside · PGM outperforming gold on relative basis
desk.sum: Platinum eased 0.8% to approximately $1,526 per ounce on Thursday, modestly tracking gold's decline but significantly outperforming on a relative basis. Platinum's industrial demand profile — hydrogen electrolysis, auto catalysts — continues to limit downside compared with pure precious metals. The WPIC supply deficit narrative remains constructive for the longer-term outlook. South African mine supply is constrained by ongoing power issues. With yields above 5% and the dollar at a 19-month high, the rate-sensitive precious metals complex remains under pressure, but platinum's industrial floor provides relative insulation.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Sharp decline tracking gold selloff · EV transition headwind persists · tested $1,000 psychological support
desk.sum: Palladium fell 3.1% to $1,008 per ounce on Thursday, sharply tracking gold's third straight session of selling. The decline brought palladium within striking distance of the $1,000 psychological support level. The structural headwind from the EV transition — battery EVs require no catalytic converter — remains the dominant longer-term dynamic. Palladium's underperformance relative to platinum reflects its greater sensitivity to the precious metals complex and weaker industrial demand profile. With yields above 5% and the dollar surging, palladium is vulnerable to a test of $1,000.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: 4 tankers hit by explosions — Iran blames 'ignored warnings' · Houthi attacks on Saudi pipeline, Yanbu, Riyadh · Trump: 'we've got their strait'
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz risk escalated sharply on Thursday. Iran's military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the strait after 'ignoring warnings' — a claim Reuters could not immediately verify. Separately, Houthi forces struck Saudi pipeline infrastructure, an oil facility in Yanbu and an Aramco building in Riyadh. Saudi air defences also intercepted two Houthi drones and destroyed two ballistic missiles aimed at Mecca. Trump declared Washington did not need a deal with Iran, saying 'we've got their strait.' The White House said the US has 'control of the Strait of Hormuz' and that Operation Economic Outcast and the new Operation Iron Gate will continue 'with full effect.' Iran's economy is described by the White House as 'collapsing.' The diplomatic track remains alive — APEC in Shenzhen November 18–19 provides a window — but the kinetic tempo is increasing.

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: Sold off on surging dollar · dollar at 19-month high · post-WASDE gains erased · ethanol production fell 1.1%
desk.sum: December corn fell 5½ cents to 442½¢ per bushel on Thursday, erasing all of Tuesday's WASDE-driven rally, as the surging dollar and rising Treasury yields overwhelmed grain markets. The dollar index hit a 19-month high, pressuring US grain export competitiveness. Ethanol production fell 1.1% to 332 million gallons. Corn's inability to hold the post-WASDE gains despite the bullish November yield cut (179.6 bushels per acre, below all analyst estimates) is a bearish signal. The USDA's Friday export sales report is expected to show 2.0–3.0 million tonnes in new corn sales. South American planting continues under generally favourable conditions.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Reversed Wednesday's break above 600¢ · dollar at 19-month high · SovEcon cuts Russian export est to 36 mmt vs USDA 39 mmt
desk.sum: December wheat fell 15¼ cents to 584¼¢ per bushel on Thursday, reversing Wednesday's psychologically important break above 600¢ in a single session. The dollar index at a 19-month high triggered likely fund selling across grains. SovEcon cut its Russian wheat export estimate to 36 million tonnes, below the USDA's 39 million tonne forecast — bullish for prices longer term but unable to offset Thursday's macro-driven selloff. Kansas City wheat fell more than Chicago (−17¼¢ to 622¼¢), suggesting some spread unwinding. The Abu Dhabi grain corridor talks remain a key potential bearish catalyst if they restart stalled Black Sea shipments.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: January front-month $12.19 · stronger dollar weighs · South American planting conditions favourable · Chinese buying muted
desk.sum: January soybeans eased 11¾ cents to $12.19 per bushel (1,219¢) on Thursday, giving back some of the post-WASDE gains. The surging dollar at a 19-month high pressured US export competitiveness, and South American supplies are more competitive than US offerings at current exchange rates. Chinese buying interest remains muted. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the WASDE report continues to provide a structural floor, but Thursday's macro-driven selloff underscored the vulnerability of grain prices to the hawkish rates environment. Soybeans held relatively better than wheat and corn on the day.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $1,993 · weakest since August · six consecutive weeks in the red · Fear & Greed at 28 'Fear' · total crypto market cap fell 4.6%
desk.sum: Bitcoin fell to approximately $72,000, down 2.8%, its weakest level since August, as the hawkish rates environment continued to crush risk assets. BTC briefly traded below $73,000 during Thursday's session before extending losses. Ethereum dropped to $1,993, down 3.0%. The Fear and Greed Index sits at 28 ('Fear'). Total crypto market capitalisation fell 4.6% over 24 hours to approximately $2.43 trillion. Bitcoin dominance is at 59.8%. Spot Bitcoin ETF outflows have continued for multiple consecutive weeks. The 10-year yield breaking above 5% and the dollar at a 19-month high are directly bearish for crypto, which trades increasingly like a risk-on / liquidity-sensitive asset. Bitcoin has now closed six consecutive weeks in the red.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM ~$32 · TTF ~€88/MWh · HH $3.31 · QatarEnergy FM through year-end · IEA: global LNG output to fall 3%
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) trades near $32 per MMBtu, modestly firmer as the broader energy complex tightened on Thursday's Saudi and Hormuz attacks. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, keeping approximately 5 bcm of supply offline. The IEA projects 2026 global LNG output will fall about 3% — the steepest annual drop on record. TTF firmed to approximately €88 per MWh in European morning trading, up 2%. Henry Hub rose to $3.31. EU storage sits below the five-year average ahead of winter. Oil's surge to $95.82 on the Saudi attacks indirectly supports LNG pricing through energy-complex correlation. The November 27 export-control deadline adds further supply-chain uncertainty.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait ~$765 · Houthi attacks on Saudi sites reduce deal odds further · 14 days to Nov 27 deadline
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. Thursday's Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure — including a pipeline pumping station and the Yanbu facility — and the tanker explosions in the Strait of Hormuz further reduce the near-term probability of Middle Eastern supply resumption. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). Chinese domestic sulfur holds near 7,200 yuan per tonne. The November 27 export-control deadline is now 14 days away. Trump's statement that Washington does not need a deal with Iran signals a hardline stance that extends the timeline for any comprehensive resolution.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · stronger dollar a mild headwind · grain selloff dampens sentiment
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds at approximately $358 per tonne. BPC's India contract remains approximately $25 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. Thursday's sharp grain selloff — wheat down 2.6%, corn down 1.5% — dampens the near-term sentiment for fertiliser demand, though the underlying WASDE-driven tighter grain balance sheets remain supportive. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions. The surging dollar at a 19-month high is a modest headwind for potash pricing.
desk.src: World Bank · Argus Media · SP Angel

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: 14 days to Nov 27 deadline · Rotterdam $18,300–19,000/t · APEC Nov 18–19 · Democrats' midterm sweep complicates talks
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near 93,500 yuan per tonne. Overseas antimony sits at approximately $18,300–19,000 per tonne in Rotterdam. The critical near-term catalyst remains the November 27 deadline — now 14 days away — when the suspension of China's export prohibition on antimony (and gallium, germanium, superhard materials) to the US expires. APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen November 18–19, providing a narrow window for Trump–Xi discussions. The Democrats' midterm sweep introduces political gridlock that could slow bilateral progress. The November 10 lapse of Announcement No. 70 has already passed with no published extension.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · 14 days to Nov 27 deadline · China domestic Ga $460/kg · Ge $4,625/kg · Alcoa Wagerup FID but not producing
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, with Chinese domestic gallium at approximately $460 per kilogram — a roughly 4.5x premium for ex-China supply. Germanium in China sits at approximately $4,625 per kilogram. The November 27 deadline is now 14 days away. APEC in Shenzhen November 18–19 provides the last major diplomatic window before the deadline. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken FID but is not yet producing. LS Cable & System and KMMI have committed $490 million to reduce reliance on Chinese rare earth magnets — part of a broader Western supply-chain de-risking effort. China produces about 98% of global gallium.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Firmer at $5.30 vs recent $5.02 · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+ supply
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds at approximately $5.30 per pound in Europe, up from recent levels near $5.02. The modest recovery reflects stabilisation in steel demand rather than a structural shift. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but large-scale adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. The November 27 export-control deadline could impact vanadium indirectly if superhard materials restrictions affect adjacent supply chains.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Continued rebound from 4-month lows · Sodexam: Ivory Coast output may fall 21–25% · El Niño 'exceptionally strong' · Harmattan risk ahead
desk.sum: ICE cocoa continued its rebound on Thursday, rising approximately 3% to above $5,200 per tonne after touching four-month lows earlier in the week. Ivory Coast's national weather agency Sodexam projected 2026/27 output could drop 21–25% due to an 'exceptionally strong El Niño event' that is shortening the rainy season. Reuters had earlier projected the mid-crop could fall 42–50% to 300,000–350,000 tonnes. Harmattan wind risk in December–January adds further supply concern. ICE warehouse inventories remain elevated at a 2.5-year high, capping the near-term recovery. The demand side is weak, with poor chocolate demand adding to exchange inventories.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: Glencore wins $900M US stockpile contract · Rotterdam standard-grade fell to $17–18/lb in late Oct · NMC-to-LFP shift continues
desk.sum: Cobalt holds near $33,525 per tonne, under continued pressure. Glencore reportedly won a US government contract to supply up to $900 million of cobalt over five years for strategic stockpiles, though volumes and pricing are unconfirmed. Rotterdam standard-grade cobalt metal fell sharply in late October to $17–18 per pound, down from $21–22 per pound. The DRC maintains export quotas of 96,600 tonnes per year through 2027. The EV battery chemistry shift from NMC to LFP continues to structurally reduce cobalt intensity. Antaike expects recycled cobalt supply to rise 26% to 50,000 tonnes and refined demand to fall 5.4% to 217,000 tonnes this year.
desk.src: Trading Economics · Argus Media · SP Angel

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Near one-year low · SMM revises Chinese stockpile to 175k t (double prior est) · Mineral Resources restarts Bald Hill · EU caps Chinese EVs at 350k/yr
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate futures edged up 0.2% to approximately ¥90,650 per tonne but remain near a one-year low. SMM revised how it compiles inventory data, adding 175,000 tonnes to Chinese stockpile estimates — roughly double the earlier figure — a bearish signal for supply-demand balance. Mineral Resources restarted the Bald Hill mine after an 18-month suspension, and Core Lithium restarted Finniss. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Goldman Sachs projects a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028. Rio Tinto is expanding its Argentine lithium projects with $1.4 billion in capex.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · oil surge supports synthetic rubber costs
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), range-bound. Southeast Asian supply remains tight with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Oil's 3.7% surge on Thursday modestly supports synthetic rubber costs, which indirectly benefits natural rubber pricing. Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. The stronger dollar at a 19-month high is a headwind for dollar-denominated commodities.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Highest since February · futures above $91 · long-term contracts near $99/lb approaching $100 · IAEA raises nuclear capacity outlook
desk.sum: Uranium spot holds at approximately $91 per pound U₃O₈, its highest level since February. Long-term contract prices continue climbing near record US levels of $99 per pound — approaching the $100 milestone. The IAEA raised its outlook for global nuclear capacity over the next two decades and counts 78 reactors under construction worldwide. Kazatomprom reported 25% year-over-year growth in sales turnover for the September quarter. Delays at Kazatomprom's TQZ sulphuric acid plant limit leaching capacity. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver, with Meta, Amazon and Microsoft signing nuclear power agreements. Italy has expressed interest in a legal framework to restore nuclear power.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: China domestic NdPr declining · ex-China premiums up to 10x · LS Cable/KMMI $490M to reduce China reliance · Lynas maintenance
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide trades near $72 per kilogram domestically in China, softening, while ex-China FOB prices remain elevated at $109–121 per kilogram. Western buyers face premiums of up to 10x Chinese prices for heavy rare earths. LS Cable & System and KMMI committed $490 million to reduce reliance on Chinese rare earth magnets. Lynas' Malaysian plant maintenance shutdown continues, and its Kalgoorlie plant is halted for power grid upgrades. China Rare Earth Group has ordered tighter executive oversight of its heavy rare earth supply chain. The November 10 lapse of Announcement No. 70 and the approaching November 27 deadline add further supply-chain uncertainty.
desk.src: SMM · Rare Earth Exchanges · SP Angel

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · miners holding firm pricing stance · CIF China flat
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, flat. Miners are holding a firm pricing stance, with Comilog (Gabonese lumps) at $4.50 per mtu and Consolidated Minerals (Australian 46% lumps) at $4.80 per mtu for recent shipments. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. The forward cost picture provides support, but soft downstream consumption limits gains. Ferro-manganese alloy in Europe holds near $1,045 per tonne.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Nearly flat amid broad selloff · dollar headwind offset by Indonesia quota tightening · surplus persists
desk.sum: LME nickel was nearly flat at approximately $16,230 per tonne on Thursday, holding steady while copper and zinc declined under the dollar's pressure. Indonesia's potential tightening of RKAB mining quotas provided a modest counterweight to the macro headwind. Nickel's surplus persists as Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions continue. SHFE nickel rose 4.7% for the week on expectations of tighter Indonesian quotas. The 10-year yield above 5% and the dollar at a 19-month high remain headwinds for industrial metals, but nickel's supply-side story is providing relative support.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Modest gain · LME official close $46,652 · inventories near 4,000 mt · Myanmar ban still constraining supply
desk.sum: LME tin edged higher to $46,652 per tonne on Thursday, gaining 0.3% in the official close despite the broader base metals pressure. LME inventory holds near 4,000 mt — low for the year — providing a floor. The cancelled warrants ratio rose to 19.5%, signalling further drawdowns ahead. Structural supply constraints persist from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. Tin's ability to post a gain on a day when copper fell 1.4% and zinc dropped 0.8% reflects its tighter fundamental supply position.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: TCs deeply negative · LME stocks fell to ~142,625 mt · dollar pressure overwhelms supply tightness
desk.sum: LME zinc fell 0.8% to $3,726 per tonne on Thursday, with the surging dollar at a 19-month high overpowering the constructive supply picture. LME inventories fell 950 tonnes to 142,625 mt, continuing the drawdown trend. Treatment charges remain deeply negative, forcing continued smelter curtailments. SMM describes the technical picture as bearish, with the 10-day moving average acting as resistance. The structural supply deficit that has driven zinc higher through 2026 remains intact, but the combination of yields above 5%, the dollar surge and fund selling is capping near-term upside.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Rotterdam APT $2,725 · China FOB $1,845 · Chongyi raised Nov long-term contract prices · Western ~3.5x China · 14 days to Nov 27
desk.sum: European tungsten APT trades at $2,725 per mtu in Rotterdam, while Chinese FOB sits at $1,845 per mtu. Western prices remain roughly 3.5 times Chinese domestic levels. Chongyi tungsten enterprises raised long-term contract prices for the first half of November, reflecting upstream tightness. The market continues to reflect the fragmentation created by China's export controls on tungsten processing technology. The November 27 deadline for the US-specific ban is now 14 days away. APEC in Shenzhen November 18–19 provides a diplomatic window, though the Democrats' midterm sweep complicates the bilateral negotiating environment.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · Houthi attacks further delay timeline · Trump: 'no deal needed' with Iran
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. Thursday's Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and Trump's statement that Washington does not need a deal with Iran further extend the timeline for any comprehensive conflict resolution and potential Ras Laffan facility repairs, currently estimated at 3–5 years. Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium. Russia's export controls extend through 2027. Commercial inventories remain at their lowest since 2008. Semiconductor fabs, MRI machines and space launch consume most demand.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · grain selloff dampens short-term fertiliser sentiment
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics. Thursday's sharp grain selloff — wheat down 2.6%, corn down 1.5% — dampens the short-term fertiliser demand outlook, though the underlying WASDE-driven tighter balance sheets remain supportive heading into the 2027 planting season. Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure further reduce the near-term probability of Hormuz reopening and Middle Eastern sulfur supply resuming.
